The r4 guide's passage (the passage this carries):
Remember When You Already Did It

My father often suggested remembering a time when I met a difficulty in a way I respected. What did I actually do? What support or conditions helped? Is one part available now? The earlier situation need not have been harder. A small real example is enough; past capacity is something to draw on, not proof that exhaustion or present limits should disappear. If no example comes, use another doorway.

append:
# Simple Practices

## Borrow Hindsight

A question to borrow from your future self: "How would I respond to this once I understood it more clearly, in balance and with compassion?" It can change how the whole thing looks. It can also just make you feel a bit more like that person, or less alone (sometimes all at once). Keep in mind it's only their best guess. No perfect Higher Self is handing down answers.

That future you also knows why you can't pull this off perfectly today. What would they do for you, if they were here? Maybe they'd be kind about it, or maybe they'd just make you some food. You can borrow a wiser future version of the other person, too, as long as you don't assume they'll end up on your side, or sorry.

## Remember When You Already Did It
brief:
- the main point: draw on your own past: remember a time you met a difficulty in a way you respect; what did you do, what support or conditions helped, and is one part available now; it needn't have been harder, a small real example is enough; past capacity is something to draw on, not proof that exhaustion or present limits should disappear; if no example comes, use another doorway.
- E159: the guide credits this to Joel's father ("My father often suggested"); the article never mentions his father and it isn't in his words, so it's left out.
